paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Sandstone is a sedimentary rock made mainly of sand-sized silicate grains, 0.0625 to 2 mm across, cemented together by another mineral. It is clastic in origin, as opposed to organic rocks like chalk and coal or chemical ones like gypsum and jasper. Sandstones make up about 20–25% of all sedimentary rocks.

paragraphs.heading: What the grains are
paragraphs.text: Most sandstone is quartz or feldspar, because these minerals resist weathering at Earth's surface better than any others. Quartz has exceptional hardness and chemical stability, which lets its grains survive being recycled several times. Feldspar grains are commonly the second most abundant. Sandstone can also hold lithic grains, pieces of ancient source rock that have not yet weathered down to single mineral grains. All other mineral grains are called accessory minerals, and they usually make up just a small percentage.

paragraphs.heading: From bedrock to buried sand
paragraphs.text: The sand grains come from bedrock that has been weathered, both physically and chemically. Weathering and erosion are fastest in areas of high relief, such as volcanic arcs. Rivers or wind carry the eroded sand from its source to places where tectonics has made room for sediment to pile up. As more sediment arrives, older sand is buried by younger sediment and undergoes diagenesis, which is mostly compaction and lithification of the sand.

paragraphs.heading: Squeezing and cementing
paragraphs.text: Compaction happens as the sand comes under growing pressure from the sediments above. Grains shift into tighter arrangements, and pore space shrinks. There can also be chemical compaction through pressure solution. The points where grains touch are under the greatest strain, and mineral under strain dissolves more readily than the rest of its grain, so the contact points dissolve away and the grains move closer. Lithification follows closely: higher temperatures at depth speed up the deposition of cement that binds the grains. The mineral dissolved from the contact points is redeposited in the pore spaces, which adds to the cement.

paragraphs.heading: How deep it happens
paragraphs.text: Most compaction and lithification take place during deeper burial. Mechanical compaction happens mainly at depths of less than 1,000 meters. Chemical compaction continues down to 2,000 meters, and most cementation takes place between 2,000 and 5,000 meters.

paragraphs.heading: Color and landscape
paragraphs.text: Like loose sand, sandstone can be given any color by impurities in its minerals. Tan, brown, yellow, red, grey, pink, white and black are the colors seen most often. Sandstone beds can form highly visible cliffs, so some regions are now strongly identified with a certain color of sandstone, as with the red rock deserts of Arches National Park. In red bed sandstones the color comes from red hematite, which likely forms in the early stages of diagenesis, at shallow depths.

paragraphs.heading: Water, oil and quartzite
paragraphs.text: Sandstone formations usually let water and other fluids percolate through, and they are porous enough to store large quantities. That makes them valuable aquifers and petroleum reservoirs. Sandstone that contains quartz can be changed into quartzite through metamorphism.
